title: Canon law
hook: the Church's law ends by saying its highest rule is the salvation of souls

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy See: the pope's office, a seat rather than a city, protected by a tiny state. Your line was the see of Peter. Did the pope turn up in your news? Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

Skip to the last page of a rulebook and you'll usually find an index, or a clause about definitions, or nothing at all. The Catholic Church's book of law is thick, numbered from start to finish, full of rules about marriages, parishes, property and courts. A reader who skips to the end finds a short canon about moving a parish priest from one parish to another. And in its very last words, the whole book says what all the other rules are for. Today, canon law.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF A RULEBOOK.` → `MARRIAGES, PARISHES, PROPERTY, COURTS.` → `THE LAST WORDS SAY WHAT IT'S FOR.`

segments.voice: First, what canon law is. It's the Church's own law, the rules by which the Catholic Church orders its life: who may be ordained, how a parish is set up, how a marriage case is heard. This week we've already leaned on it again and again: for secular institutes, the parish, the diocese and the Holy See. The Latin Church has its Code of Canon Law, and the Eastern Catholic Churches have their own code. Second, what canon law is not. It isn't the faith itself, and it isn't a list of everything holy. It's more like the plumbing and wiring of a house: unglamorous, mostly unnoticed, and badly missed when it fails. Third, that last canon. It deals with a hard moment: a bishop needs to transfer a pastor who doesn't want to go. The canon tells the bishop to act with fairness, what canonists call canonical equity, and to keep before his eyes the salvation of souls, which, it says, must always be the supreme law in the Church. In Latin, the key words are salus animarum, the salvation of souls. So the book ends not with a penalty but with a purpose. Last, why it matters on a Tuesday. Every rule in the book is meant to be read in that light. Jesus describes himself in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, this way: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." Canon law is the Church's attempt to organize shepherding, and its final line reminds every bishop, priest and judge that the sheep are the point.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S OWN LAW.` · `PLUMBING AND WIRING, NOT THE HOUSE.` · `THE LAST CANON: THE SALVATION OF SOULS.` · `THE SHEEP ARE THE POINT.` · then, large: `THE SUPREME LAW IN THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read that last canon. Settle, and breathe. Let its idea come to you slowly, the way it's written: fairness, and before your eyes, the salvation of souls, the supreme law. Now think of one rule you keep at home or at work, a house rule, a policy, a habit. Ask what it's for. Is it still serving the people it was made for? If you pray, you can bring that rule, and the people it touches, to God. If you don't, sit with the question. After the bell, find the last canon of the Code and read it whole. The bell holds the time.
Canon law. The Church's own law, whose final canon names the salvation of souls as its supreme law. Today's word.
Your line: for souls. Today, when a rule gets in your way or you enforce one on someone else, ask the last canon's question: who is this for? Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Catholic dioceses have canon lawyers and church courts, called tribunals, that apply canon law, including in marriage cases. Priests and bishops study it as part of their training.

notes: Editor pass: 'we've already met it twice' was a wrong count (canon law was cited on days 1412–1415); now names the days without a number.

Canon 1752 paraphrased: in cases of transfer, canon 1747 is applied, canonical equity is observed, and the salvation of souls, which must always be the supreme law in the Church, is kept before one's eyes. Latin: 'salute animarum, quae in Ecclesia suprema semper lex esse debet, prae oculis habita.' Confirm; the original game gives the nominative 'salus animarum'.
'Numbered from start to finish' avoids stating the number of canons, per the claims rule.
'Canonical equity' explained as fairness: simplification; confirm.
The Greek origin of 'canon' (rule, measuring rod) is deliberately left out under the claims rule.
